analysis.one_liner: Makes AM/FM radio pay royalties to performers and labels for playing their recordings, with flat fees for small stations.
analysis.headline: The bill drew bipartisan sponsorship from 15 House members but died without a single committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, AM/FM radio stations play recorded songs without paying the performers or record labels, while satellite and internet radio do pay. This bill would extend that payment requirement to broadcast radio: a board would set royalty rates for large stations, while stations with less than $1.5 million in annual revenue would pay small flat fees between $10 and $500 a year. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Recording artists and record labels, who would collect royalties when broadcast radio plays their songs; under existing distribution rules, featured performers receive 45% of such royalties and copyright owners 50%. Small and public radio stations also benefit from capped flat fees far below market rates.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public performance right in sound recordings for all audio transmissions, so AM/FM stations would need a license to play copyrighted recordings instead of playing them free [S2].

Protects small broadcasters: stations under $1.5 million in revenue pay flat fees of $10, $100, or $500 per year depending on size, and the owner's total revenue must be under $10 million to qualify [S3].
States that nothing in the bill may reduce songwriter royalties, keeping the new payments separate from the existing song-composition royalties [S3].

Directs the Copyright Royalty Judges to weigh whether radio airplay promotes or substitutes for record sales when setting rates, addressing broadcasters' argument that airplay is free advertising [S2,S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial AM/FM radio stations, especially large station groups, which would pay board-set royalties for the first time in roughly a century; the cost would come out of station operating budgets and could pressure smaller marginal stations despite the flat-fee cap.

drawbacks.text: Broadcast radio would face a new mandatory cost that its terrestrial competitors' exemption has historically avoided, and stations in thin local markets could see programming cuts even with the flat fees [S2].

Roughly half of the new royalties (50%) would go to copyright owners, i.e. record labels, with 45% to featured performers and 5% to session and background musicians under the existing distribution formula, so much of the money would reach large labels rather than working artists.

The bill also requires services with direct-licensing deals to route 50% of those payments through the artist distribution collective, a change that could disrupt existing private deals between digital services and labels [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: performers earn nothing when broadcast radio plays their recordings even though internet and satellite radio pay. The carve-outs for small and public stations and the instruction to weigh radio's promotional value are genuine cost-limiting features, which is why it drew members from both parties. The main objection is that half the money would flow to record labels rather than performers, and that any new cost on radio ultimately pressures an industry already losing listeners to streaming.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on February 2, 2023 with original cosponsors Reps. Nadler, Lieu, and McClintock, a Republican-led bill backed by the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee [S3,S5].
Fourteen members cosponsored the bill, 12 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4].

The bill's only action was referral to the House Committee on the Judiciary on February 2, 2023; no subcommittee or full-committee markup, no hearing listed, and no floor vote ever occurred through the end of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: AM/FM radio broadcasters, particularly large station groups, are better off because the bill died: they keep the long-standing exemption and continue paying nothing to performers or labels for playing their recordings. The committee's failure to act, not a vote, decided the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Radio broadcasters who keep paying nothing

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: a Republican sponsor and 14 cosponsors split 12 Democrats to 2 Republicans, and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote on either side.

industries.note: For roughly a century broadcast radio has played recordings without paying performers or labels; this bill ends that exemption, with board-set rates for large station groups and flat fees of $10-$500 for small stations. Stations profit from using recordings for free, so their interest in keeping the status quo runs against the performers' interest in being paid.

As copyright owners of sound recordings, labels would receive 50% of the new broadcast royalties under existing distribution rules. The money comes from radio companies rather than directly from the public.
Featured performers would receive 45% and nonfeatured musicians 5% of the new royalties, income they currently earn from streaming and satellite radio but not from AM/FM airplay.

Stations under $1.5 million in revenue would face a new cost, but it is capped at $10-$500 per year, far below what market-rate licensing might otherwise cost them, so the bill shields them relative to large broadcasters.

industries.industry: Digital music services with direct licenses
industries.note: The bill requires services holding direct licenses with labels to route 50% of those payments through the artist distribution collective, adding artists' share to existing deals but constraining private contracting.
